content: 1. Monitoring of HIV treatment using nucleic acid testing (NAT) is recommended for individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Routine viral load monitoring should be conducted at six months, 12 months, and then annually if the patient is stable on ART. This aligns with routine monitoring and evaluation schedules. 2. In settings where routine viral load monitoring is available, CD4 cell count monitoring can be discontinued for individuals established on ART. However, in settings where viral load testing is not routinely available, CD4 count and clinical monitoring should be used to diagnose treatment failure. 3. Dried blood spot specimens, derived from venous or capillary whole blood, can be used to measure HIV viral load. A threshold of 1,000 copies/mL is recommended to define virological failure when using dried blood spot samples, though plasma specimens are preferred for viral load testing. 4. For individuals initiating first-line ART with pre-treatment HIV drug resistance to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs), NNRTI-containing regimens should be avoided. In countries where pre-treatment NNRTI resistance exceeds 10%, NNRTI-based ART should not be used. 5. A comprehensive care package, including screening, treatment, and/or prophylaxis for major opportunistic infections, rapid ART initiation, and intensified adherence support, should be provided to individuals with advanced HIV disease. 6. For suspected cryptococcal meningitis in individuals with HIV, a lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure measurement and rapid cryptococcal antigen assay is the preferred diagnostic approach. If antigen assays are unavailable, CSF India ink examination is recommended. 7. Cryptococcal antigen screening followed by pre-emptive antifungal therapy is recommended for individuals with HIV and CD4 counts <100 cells/mm³ to prevent invasive cryptococcal disease. This may also be considered for CD4 counts <200 cells/mm³. 8. The preferred induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis in HIV patients is amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg/day) combined with flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day in four divided doses). Alternative regimens include fluconazole (1,200 mg daily) with flucytosine or amphotericin B with fluconazole. 9. For the consolidation phase of cryptococcal meningitis treatment, fluconazole (400–800 mg daily) is recommended for eight weeks following induction therapy. Maintenance therapy with fluconazole (200 mg daily) is recommended thereafter. 10. Routine use of adjunctive systemic corticosteroids during the induction phase of cryptococcal meningitis treatment is not recommended due to increased risks. 11. ART initiation should be deferred by 4–6 weeks after starting antifungal treatment in individuals with cryptococcal meningitis to reduce mortality risk. 12. Disseminated histoplasmosis in individuals with HIV should be diagnosed by detecting circulating Histoplasma antigens. Amphotericin B (1 mg/kg daily) is recommended for two weeks as induction therapy, followed by itraconazole for maintenance. 13. For mild to moderate histoplasmosis, itraconazole (200 mg three times daily for three days, then 200 mg twice daily) is recommended. Maintenance therapy with itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) for 12 months is advised, though shorter durations may be considered if the patient is clinically stable and virologically suppressed on ART. 14. ART should be initiated as soon as possible in individuals with disseminated histoplasmosis without central nervous system involvement. 15. For individuals co-infected with tuberculosis (TB), HIV, and histoplasmosis, TB therapy should follow WHO guidelines. 16. Children and adolescents with HIV should engage in at least 60 minutes of moderateto vigorous-intensity physical activity daily, including muscleand bone-strengthening activities at least three days per week. Sedentary time, particularly recreational screen time, should be limited. 17. Adults, including older adults, should perform at least 150–300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity or 75–150 minutes of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity weekly. Muscle-strengthening activities involving all major muscle groups should be done on two or more days per week. 18. Older adults should include multicomponent physical activities emphasizing balance and strength training at least three days per week to enhance functional capacity and prevent falls. 19. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for individuals with severe or advanced HIV disease (WHO stage 3 or 4) and/or CD4 counts ≤350 cells/mm³. In high-prevalence settings for malaria or severe bacterial infections, co-trimoxazole should be initiated regardless of CD4 count or WHO stage. 20. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis may be discontinued in clinically stable adults on ART with evidence of immune recovery and viral suppression. However, in high-prevalence settings for malaria or bacterial infections, prophylaxis should continue regardless of CD4 count or clinical stage. 21. Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis is recommended for all children with HIV, with priority given to those under five years old or with severe or advanced HIV disease. In low-prevalence settings, prophylaxis may be discontinued for children aged five years or older who are clinically stable and virologically suppressed on ART with CD4 counts >350 cells/mm³.
